title: Drills
summary: Runs of exercises over a lesson's own items, graded by the share answered right.
description:
A drill practises a handful of items: words, sentences or a dialogue. Its exercises are built fresh each time from the items and their history, so a brand-new word is shown on a card first, a word seen before is recognised among choices, and one that has held up has to be typed from memory.

Inside a drill every word and sentence has its own review history. That history decides how hard the exercise is; when the lesson itself comes back is decided by the lesson's schedule.

requirements.text: A word never answered is shown on a card that is only read and then asked by multiple choice; one answered before is asked by multiple choice; one answered right on three different days in a row has to be typed.
Typed answers ignore case, punctuation and spacing, and accept Polish letters typed without their marks: `czesc` counts as `cześć`.
A typed answer one letter off a word of four letters or more is almost right.
A dictation or spoken sentence of three words or more with one word wrong is almost right.
An almost-right answer is logged as a mistake, earns half the XP, counts as half right in the drill's score, and brings the item back sooner instead of starting its reviews over.
A drill passes at 85% right; a drill of three to six scored cards also passes with a single miss, or two almost-right answers.
A drill with 60% or more right that does not pass is a partial; less is a fail.
An ace in a drill is a pass with no almost-right answers and at least 95% of the scored cards fully right.
Cards that are only read (a new word, a dialogue to read, a story panel) are not scored, and a drill with nothing scored is not graded.
A sentence whose words change their ending is built from tiles in dictionary form, and the learner picks the ending on each tile; a sentence without stored endings is built by plain ordering.
A wrong answer on a word shows example sentences for it: made once by a model and kept, or, without a key, taken from the learner's own courses.
After a word or sentence card is answered, the learner can talk about it with the tutor straight from the exercise; that chat has its own model setting and otherwise uses the tutor's model.
Each word's and sentence's review interval grows with right answers on different days, to at most 365 days; an item counts once a day.

questions: The README says an ace needs every answer fully right; the code gives an ace at 95% fully right with no almost-right answers, so a drill of 20 cards or more can have one miss. Which is meant?
